bollymeter.basis: A generously budgeted (approx. $33 million) supernatural thriller whose world-building and leads carry real weight, even when the 16-episode runtime strains the central mystery. Audience Popcornmeter on Rotten Tomatoes sat at 89%, reflecting strong fan enthusiasm for the reincarnation mythology.

seasons.review_body: Bulgasal: Immortal Souls arrived in late 2021 as one of Studio Dragon's most ambitious genre swings - a $33-million supernatural thriller spanning 600 years of reincarnation and vengeance. The show's lush production design and unusual decision to interweave Joseon-era flashbacks with a contemporary Seoul thriller were its most discussed formal qualities. Lee Jin-wook grounds the immortal bulgasal with quiet menace, and Kwon Nara handles the dual-timeline trauma with discipline. The series struggles in its middle stretch, where the mythology grows dense and forward momentum stalls. The 89% Rotten Tomatoes audience score reflects real enthusiasm for the show's mythological ambition. A rewarding binge for viewers willing to invest in the world-building.

# Bulgasal Immortal Souls S01E01: "Episode 1" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

A baby is cursed before he can choose a side. The village does not treat him like an infant. It treats him like a door left open for a monster. By the time the crowd insists the boy must die to stop Bulgasal from coming every night, the premiere has shown its hand. Immortality drives the myth, but human fear gives the opener its first weapon. The episode works best when the curse infects ordinary people before the monster takes over the frame.

## The Curse Arrives Before the Character

The premiere opens with lore so direct it lands like a carved warning. Six hundred years ago, non-human beings called Monsters lived on the land. Then comes the defining rule: **Bulgasal** declares, "I cannot be killed and cannot die as I am Bulgasal." The line does necessary genre work. It tells the viewer what kind of creature is being invoked, what kind of death will not solve the problem, and why the story can stretch across lifetimes.

The risk is obvious. The early minutes carry a heavy load of explanation: narrator, curse, monster logic, doomed birth, invulnerability. That is a lot of myth to stack before the human drama has room to breathe. The episode asks for trust through dense statements, which makes the first act feel more like prophecy than life.

Still, the bluntness has purpose. The premiere wants Bulgasal to feel like a weather system. The child is cursed before he has agency. The village has an explanation before it has compassion. Fear gets a name, and once it has a name, everyone can pretend cruelty is practical. That is the hour's strongest early idea.

## A Village Turns Fear Into Policy

The village scenes are where the premiere starts to bite. **Pal-bong**'s wife and children are dead. The cursed boy becomes the easiest answer to a grief too large for the village to carry cleanly. At 20 minutes in, the demand is no longer whispered. The villagers insist they must kill him to stop Bulgasal from coming every night.

That exchange is the episode's first moral test, staged through threat-led dialogue instead of delicate argument. Someone warns that "it will come knocking on your doors every night." The line matters because it turns superstition into schedule. Bulgasal is no distant myth in that moment. It becomes the thing that will arrive after sunset, again and again, until the village offers a sacrifice.

The writing is sharpest here because nobody needs a grand speech about panic. The crowd's logic is ugly enough. A child is reduced to a solution. Death is presented as village maintenance. The hour understands that mobs rarely call themselves mobs. They call themselves responsible.

The limitation is emotional distance around the loss itself. Pal-bong's dead family is a crucial trigger, but the episode moves quickly from fact to reaction. That keeps the dread moving. It also makes the grief more functional than felt. The scene lands as social horror before it lands as personal tragedy.

## General Dan Geuk Names the Problem

**General Dan Geuk of Goryeo** gives the premiere its most interesting contradiction. He wants to stop the slaughter of the cursed child, yet he lives inside the same cursed logic as everyone else. He does not dismiss the village's fear. He redirects it, disciplines it, and takes responsibility for the boy.

That choice becomes physical when he intervenes and names the child. "Your name shall be Hwal." It is a small line with a large function. A mob sees a curse. The General forces a person into the frame. Naming the boy does not erase the danger, and the episode knows that. Dan Geuk protects the child while warning that the curse persists until the boy dies.

That makes him more compelling than a pure savior figure. He is a man trying to impose order on a world that keeps answering with blood. His later talk about battlefield life being over and his adopted son being blessed by Bulgasal adds another layer of irony. The General tries to retire one kind of violence, but the old monster story keeps recruiting him back.

The episode's craft improves around him because action and belief finally collide. He does not just explain the curse. He makes a decision under it. That is where the premiere stops sounding like lore delivery and starts behaving like drama.

## Hwal Cannot Outrun the Name

Once the boy becomes **Hwal**, the premiere gains a spine. His contradiction is clean: he wants to let go of Bulgasal and stop Monster hunting, yet the hour keeps tying him back to the curse. The name that saves him also marks him. The General's intervention gives him identity, but it cannot give him freedom.

This is where the episode's time-span ambition starts to show. A cursed baby. An adopted son. Battlefield exhaustion. Monster hunting. The pull of Bulgasal. The premiere is not content with one crisis. It wants the opening hour to feel like an origin wound, the kind that hardens into destiny.

That ambition creates a pacing problem. The episode moves from myth to village terror to adopted identity to hunting stakes with the solemnity of a saga. Some transitions have force. Others feel like the show placing stones for a longer road. The mood stays coherent, but the weight of setup is visible.

Still, Hwal's arc gives the hour an emotional engine. He is no longer only the boy everyone feared. He becomes the man forced to face the thing that fear named for him. The premiere is most persuasive when Hwal's fate is treated as a debt other people wrote in his blood.

## The Monster Finally Steps Out of Rumor

The late stretch tightens because the episode shifts from forecast to confrontation. the declaration arrives: they are here to kill Bulgasal, and anyone who stands in the way is threatened. The hour has spent so much time letting Bulgasal exist as story, curse, excuse, and dread that this move toward direct violence feels earned.

The simple line "It is here" works because the show has prepared the silence around it. The late-scene pauses matter. After the front-loaded explanation, the episode finally trusts short lines and held tension. The monster story becomes cleaner when people stop describing fear and start reacting to its arrival.

Then the final reincarnation threat widens the frame again. Bulgasal says she will find the man no matter how many times he is reincarnated. It is a strong closing engine because it turns a chase into a curse with memory. Death will not settle the account. Time will not bury it. The premiere begins with immortality as a rule and ends with immortality as revenge.

That is the hour's best structural move. The opening says Bulgasal cannot die. The ending says the grudge cannot die either. The episode over-explains its mythology early, but it understands what the mythology is for: pursuit without expiry.

## The Verdict

"Episode 1" is a heavy, gripping opener that sometimes lets lore walk ahead of feeling. The exposition is dense, especially in the first stretch, and the dead family beat needed more emotional space before becoming fuel for the village's violence. But the craft steadies once the cursed child becomes Hwal, and General Dan Geuk's intervention gives the hour a human contradiction strong enough to carry the myth.

The premiere's real achievement is turning Bulgasal into more than a creature. Bulgasal functions as rumor, justification, curse, and finally a revenge that promises to survive reincarnation. As a season opener, it plants large questions with confidence: whether the boy can die, whether death would help, and whether a grudge this old can be broken without creating another monster.

Written by BollyAI, reviewed by our editorial team.

verdict.one_liner: A heavy but gripping opener turns curse lore into social violence, then lets reincarnation sharpen the knife.
